name: Chrystia Freeland
role: Canadian politician and journalist: MP since 2013, Minister of Foreign Affairs 2017-19, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance 2019-24
summary: Freeland, a former journalist, set out as Foreign Minister a foreign policy built on a rules-based order, free trade, NATO's Article 5 and the principled use of force; she has criticised state control of the press in Russia and named climate change as the first new imperative.

sources.title: Address by Minister Freeland on Canada's foreign policy priorities, House of Commons, 6 June 2017 (Global Affairs Canada, canada.ca)
sources.author: Chrystia Freeland

sources.title: Budget 2022, Chapter 6: Health (Department of Finance Canada; the budget tabled by Chrystia Freeland as Minister of Finance, 7 April 2022; archived page)
sources.author: Department of Finance Canada

universal-healthcare.rationale: In Budget 2022, which she tabled as Finance Minister, the government proposed $5.3 billion over five years (then $1.7 billion ongoing) to provide dental care for Canadians, after noting that a third of Canadians have no dental insurance, and committed to a Canada Pharmacare bill to be passed by the end of 2023 with a national formulary and bulk purchasing plan.

free-trade.rationale: In her 6 June 2017 address she said of the rules-based order: 'Another key benefit for Canada from an international system based on rules, is of course free trade', adding that 'beggar-thy-neighbour policies hit middle powers soonest and hardest' and 'Rising trade barriers hurt the people they are intended to help. They curb growth, stifle innovation and kill employment'.

nation-first.rationale: She told the House that humankind had learned 'that the narrow pursuit of national self-interest, the law of the jungle, led to nothing but carnage and poverty', and that Canada, 'a middle power living next to the world's only super power', has a huge interest in an order 'in which might is not always right'.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: In her 6 June 2017 address she named 'the fight against climate change first among' the new shared human imperatives that 'call for renewed, uncommon resolve', and cited the Paris agreement, 'with 194 signatories', as an example of global co-operation.

party-controls-media.rationale: As a journalist on CNN in 2003 she said that in Russia 'the press is being controlled and is being restricted because Putin and his people want to make sure they remain in power', and that Russia's direction toward a society where the public space is dominated by the state means 'press freedoms are very real'.

collective-defense.rationale: In the same address she said Canada's commitment to the Transatlantic Alliance is shown by CETA and 'our military deployment this summer to Latvia', and 'There can be no clearer sign that NATO and Article 5 are at the heart of Canada's national security policy'.

arms-reduction.rationale: In her 2017 address she said 'Canadian diplomacy and development sometimes require the backing of hard power. Force is of course always a last resort. But the principled use of force, together with our allies and governed by international law, is part of our history and must be part of our future. To have that capacity requires a substantial investment', which looks to arms for an international role as well as for national safety.

notes: A first audit from her 6 June 2017 foreign-policy address to the House of Commons and a 2003 CNN interview, with the other CNN and NPR interviews in the local corpus (2000-2018) searched for further positions. Seven statements answered: six from her words and universal-healthcare from Budget 2022 (chapter 6, tabled by her as Finance Minister). Her acts are record for a later pass: as Finance Minister, the rest of Budget 2022 (only chapters 1 and 6 were looked at) and Budgets 2021-24 and the Fall Economic Statements; as MP, her votes in the House of Commons; and her books (Plutocrats, Sale of the Century), on the economy and inequality. The uncertainty rule is not met.
